name: Nora Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Fairlow for seven. It's my cousin Martin's in-laws' farm, out on the Ashby road: eight thousand free-range hens, potatoes, and a few beef cattle in the back barn. First job is the hen houses, picking up the floor eggs the girls lay in the wrong place, checking for dead birds, sorting the water lines. Then the egg room with Janet, then potatoes or whatever Martin needs. I've done two years. Before that I ran the shop floor at a garden centre for sixteen years until it shut.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the routine. Same houses, same order, same time, every day. The hens like it too, they get funny if you change anything, and so do I. What wears me out is being the one who doesn't know. Janet can grade an egg by holding it up to the light for half a second. I'm still squinting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, told you. Everyone at the garden centre was going on about AI two years before it closed, and it closed because of the bypass, not computers. I'd say that to Janet in the egg room and leave it there. I'm not on any of the online stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think, good, that's one less thing. I've just got the hang of the hen houses. I don't want anyone changing them now. I'm not against new things for other people, I just don't want them in my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Same as now. Keep turning up, keep putting money by like we do, keep learning off Janet. Maybe in spring I'd ask Martin if I can do more on the potatoes, because the grading line there is something I'd like to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled. Like when you get the last hen house done and it's still light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want new things in your day. Have there been any at Fairlow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin put in a new egg counter last year that talks to his phone. I didn't mind that, it was in his office. What I'd mind is something walking about in my hen houses that I have to keep out of the way of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture you'd still keep an eye on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, maybe. Feed's gone up every year. If the AI does anything it'd be the big egg packers using it to squeeze farms. But that happens anyway, with or without computers.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, and remind Janet that the garden centre closed because of the bypass, not computers. I'm not on any online stuff, so that's where it ends.
S0.think: Good, that's one less thing to worry about. I've just got the hang of the hen houses and I don't want anything changed now; new things are fine, just not in my day.
S0.do: Carries on as now, keeps saving at the usual rate and keeps learning egg grading from Janet. Asks in spring to work more on the potato grading line.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like finishing the last hen house before dark.
S0.quote: What I'd mind is something walking about in my hen houses that I have to keep out of the way of.
S0.fieldNote: Nora values routine above almost everything and says so with good humour. She doesn't blame AI or anyone in particular, preferring plain business explanations like the bypass. She's comfortable with technology that stays in someone else's office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, isn't it. Farms have always brought in new machines, my grandad went from horses to a tractor. I wouldn't moan in public, there's no point. I'd say we'll see how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd bother me more than I'd let on. Floor eggs, dead birds, water lines, that's all stuff I've read a robot can do, a little one that drives round the shed. Martin's a sensible man, if it's cheaper he'll buy it. I wouldn't blame him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait the first year and see what Martin does. If a robot came into the hen houses, I'd ask to move fully onto the potatoes and the cattle. And if Fairlow didn't need me, there's plenty of farms round here, I'd ask at the Pattersons' or the dairy over the hill. I'd also put a bit extra by each month, just to feel better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a sound in the car you hope goes away by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask at other farms. Is that easy for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easy. I hate starting again, I did it two years ago and it took a year to stop feeling stupid. But there's work about. Steve always says there's never a shortage of muck to shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn to run the robot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they put a paper in front of me with the buttons, maybe. I'm not having it on my phone. I've got a phone for texting Steve and the school and that's it.

S1.say: I'd say it's just business, the same as when my grandad went from horses to a tractor. I wouldn't moan in public; I'd say we'll see how it goes.
S1.think: It'd bother me more than I'd show, because the little shed robots can already do floor eggs and dead birds. If it's cheaper Martin will buy one, and I wouldn't blame him.
S1.do: Waits a year to see what Martin buys, then asks to move onto potatoes and cattle if a robot takes the hen houses. Would ask at nearby farms if Fairlow didn't need her, and adds a little extra to savings each month.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in the car she hopes will fix itself.
S1.quote: Floor eggs, dead birds, water lines, that's all stuff I've read a robot can do, a little one that drives round the shed.
S1.fieldNote: Publicly she shrugs it off as business, while privately she's already worked out that her exact tasks are the ones a shed robot does. She blames no one, not even the farmer who'd buy it. Her fallback is the many farms nearby, though she dreads starting again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should have seen it coming. I don't know who, the government, the companies, all of them. But I'd keep it short, because I don't know enough to argue about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's Steve as well. He drives for the grain merchant, and if lorries drive themselves he's done too. Two years. We've got my gran's money and our savings, more than a year of bills, but I'd lie awake doing sums. I don't have a plan for this. I don't know what I'd even learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need straight away. The new kitchen can wait, the holiday can wait. I'd keep working at Fairlow as long as Martin would have me, and if it went, I'd ask my sister about work at her shop in town. Mostly I'd sit tight and see, because I don't know which way to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'm not someone who panics, but this I'd feel in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lie awake doing sums. What sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How long the mortgage runs if neither of us is earning. About fourteen months, I think, if we're careful, more with gran's money. Then what? That's the sum that doesn't finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Callum and Rosie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum's fourteen, he'd tell me, Mum, chill. Rosie's eleven, she'd worry about the hens. I'd tell them we're fine for now, and I'd mean for now.

S2.say: I'd say it came too fast and that somebody, government or companies, should have seen it coming. I'd keep it short, because I don't feel I know enough to argue.
S2.think: Steve's lorry job would go too, so it's both of us in two years. We've savings and my gran's money for more than a year, but I'd lie awake doing sums with no plan.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending at once, shelving the kitchen and holiday. Stays at Fairlow as long as possible, then asks her sister about work in her shop in town, while mostly sitting tight.
S2.feel: Frightened, a feeling she says she'd carry in her stomach.
S2.quote: Then what? That's the sum that doesn't finish.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline hits both household wages, and her resistance to change leaves her with no clear move. She leans on family for a fallback job and on her inheritance for time. The fear is real despite the savings, because she can't see an end to the sum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the people in charge to sort out what happens to the rest of us. I'd say it calmly. There's no point getting worked up in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be just about properly good at the job by then. That's the bit that stings. But it gives Steve and me time to pay a chunk off the house, and I'd sleep better than with two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd overpay the mortgage every month, maybe four hundred extra, and keep the rest of gran's money where it is. I'd keep working, same as now. Around year three, if Fairlow had robots in, I'd go and look for something with people in it, maybe the school kitchen, Rosie's school is always advertising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But it's the kind I can live with. Like waiting for test results you're fairly sure are fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the school kitchen. Does that appeal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I like being outside. But there'd still be dinner ladies, I reckon. Or maybe not. I don't know. I'd find out when I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the new machines in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that's daft. But I'd rather do something else than learn to babysit a robot. I'm forty-three, I've changed jobs once, I'm not doing computers.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for the people in charge to sort out what happens to the rest of us. I'd say it calmly, without getting worked up in public.
S3.think: In five years I'd only just be good at the job, and that stings. But it gives Steve and me time to pay off part of the house, so I'd sleep better than with two.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by around four hundred a month and leaves the inheritance untouched. Keeps working as now, and around year three looks for work with people, such as the school kitchen.
S3.feel: Anxious in a way she can live with, like waiting for test results she's fairly sure are fine.
S3.quote: I'd rather do something else than learn to babysit a robot.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets her turn worry into paying down the mortgage. She's firm about not learning the machines and calls it daft herself. Her fallback job choice is about people, though she's honest that she doesn't know if it's safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, well, that's a career for some people. Plenty of time. I'd say it to Janet and we'd probably both agree we'd be retired or near enough by then. We wouldn't, but we'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm fifty-three, the house is nearly paid, the kids are grown. I think we'd be all right. I'd worry more for Callum and Rosie, starting out into that. For me it'd be a long goodbye to the hens, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep saving. I'd sit down with Callum about what he does after school, because he's thinking about mechanics. Maybe I'd tell him look at something with people, like nursing. I wouldn't change much for myself in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly for the kids. For me, settled enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you and Janet would say you'd be retired. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd be fifty-three and Steve wants to work till he drops. We'd be working at something. I just don't know what, and with ten years I don't have to know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Janet. She's sixty, she's done eggs her whole life, she's got nothing else. I'd want Martin to keep her on to the end. I think he would. He's decent.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a whole career for some people, plenty of time. Janet and I would agree we'd be retired by then, even though we wouldn't be.
S4.think: At fifty-three with the house nearly paid and the kids grown, I think we'd be all right. For me it's a long goodbye to the hens, not a cliff; the kids are the real worry.
S4.do: Carries on working and saving with little change in the first year. Talks to her son Callum about his plans after school and steers him from mechanics towards work with people, such as nursing.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the children, settled enough for herself.
S4.quote: For me it'd be a long goodbye to the hens, not a cliff.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her worry moves from her own job to her children's futures. She doesn't feel she has to decide anything yet, which suits her. She trusts her employer to look after older staff like Janet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it'd be Steve and me both, and I wouldn't know what to do. What would help is somebody local telling you plainly what jobs are still there, in this area, not on some website. A person at the job centre who knows farms. And some help with the mortgage if both wages go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people actually like about their jobs. Everyone asks about money. I like the hens' noise first thing, that little grumble when you open the door. A robot wouldn't miss that, but I would.

headlineQuote: I like the hens' noise first thing, that little grumble when you open the door. A robot wouldn't miss that, but I would.
portrait: Nora Baker is 43 and two years into farm work at a family hen and potato farm, after sixteen years running a garden centre shop floor that closed. She loves routine, doesn't use AI and only texts on her phone, and she treats change as plain business rather than anyone's fault. Her savings and an inheritance from her gran give her a cushion, but her husband drives lorries, so the fast AGI scenario would hit both wages and leaves her frightened and without a plan. With more time she pays down the mortgage, refuses to learn the machines, and turns her worry towards her children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit her and her lorry-driver husband at once and she wouldn't know what to do.
whatWouldHelp: A local person at the job centre who knows farms and can say plainly which jobs are still there, and some help with the mortgage if both wages go.
